intro: This branch covers the hands-on side of geometry: angles, area, volume and circles, plus the Pythagorean theorem, a famous rule for right triangles. It is about measuring and working things out, from carpeting a room to filling a can; proving why the rules are true comes later, in Era V.

III.8.01.what: Using the ways angles fit together, like two angles on a straight line always adding up to 180 degrees.

levels.a: Checks whether two angles are complementary, meaning they add up to 90 degrees.
levels.b: Finds angles that are supplementary, meaning they add up to 180 degrees.
levels.c: Finds all four angles where two straight lines cross, since opposite angles are equal.
levels.d: Writes and solves an equation to find a missing angle.

III.8.02.what: Finding the angles formed when one line crosses two parallel lines (lines that never meet).

levels.a: Finds the matching angle in the same position at the other crossing.
levels.b: Finds angle pairs on opposite sides of the crossing line, which are equal.
levels.c: Finds angle pairs on the same side between the parallel lines, which add to 180 degrees.
levels.d: Finds all eight angles from just one.

III.8.03.what: Using the fact that the three angles inside any triangle always add up to 180 degrees.

levels.a: Checks whether three angles could belong to a triangle.
levels.b: Finds a missing angle in a triangle.
levels.c: Uses an angle outside the triangle, which equals the two far inside angles added together.
levels.d: Finds a missing angle in two steps, such as working out a second angle first.
levels.e: Finds a triangle's angles when they are given as a ratio, such as 9 to 7 to 4.
levels.f: Finds the angle where two corner-splitting lines (angle bisectors) meet inside a triangle.

III.8.04.what: Finding the area (the space inside) of a parallelogram, a slanted rectangle.

levels.a: Cuts a triangle off one end and slides it over to make a rectangle.
levels.b: Finds the area by multiplying the base by the height.
levels.c: Picks the true straight-up height and ignores the slanted side.
levels.d: Works backwards from the area to find a missing height or base.

III.8.05.what: Finding the area of a triangle, which is half of a matching parallelogram.

levels.a: Sees that a triangle is half of a parallelogram.
levels.b: Finds the area as half of base times height.
levels.c: Finds the area of a wide-angled triangle whose height falls outside it.
levels.d: Works backwards from the area to find a missing base or height.

III.8.06.what: Finding the area of a trapezoid, a four-sided shape with one pair of parallel sides.

levels.a: Splits a trapezoid into a rectangle and triangles and adds their areas.
levels.b: Averages the two parallel sides, then multiplies by the height.
levels.c: Uses the trapezoid formula, ignoring measurements it does not need.
levels.d: Works backwards from the area to find a missing side.

III.8.07.what: Finding the area of irregular shapes by breaking them into simpler pieces.

levels.a: Splits a shape into two rectangles and finds each area.
levels.b: Finds the total area of a shape made of several parts.
levels.c: Subtracts a cut-out hole from a larger area.
levels.d: Finds the area of a shape drawn on a coordinate grid.
levels.e: Finds both the area and the perimeter after a notch or corner is cut from a rectangle.
levels.f: Finds the area of a tilted square drawn inside a square, by cutting off four corner triangles.

III.8.08.what: Naming the parts of a circle and meeting pi, the special number (about 3.14) that links a circle's width to its distance around.

levels.a: Names the center, radius (center to edge), and diameter (all the way across).
levels.b: Uses the fact that the diameter is twice the radius.
levels.c: Names a chord (a straight line across) and an arc (a curved piece of the edge).
levels.d: Divides the distance around a circle by its size to see pi appear.

III.8.09.what: Finding the circumference, the distance around a circle.

levels.a: Estimates the distance around from the width, using pi.
levels.b: Finds the exact distance around from the radius, leaving the answer in terms of pi.
levels.c: Works backwards from the distance around to find the width.
levels.d: Turns an exact answer in terms of pi into a decimal using 3.14.

III.8.10.what: Finding the area inside a circle: pi times the radius times the radius.

levels.a: Finds the exact area from the radius.
levels.b: Finds the area from the diameter, halving it first.
levels.c: Finds the area of half and quarter circles.
levels.d: Works backwards from the area to find the size of the circle.
levels.e: Finds the area of a ring between two circles with the same center.
levels.f: Finds the area of a circle drawn around a square, using the square's diagonal.

III.8.11.what: Finding surface area: the total area of all the flat faces of a 3D shape, like wrapping paper for a box.

levels.a: Picks a net (the flat pattern that folds into a shape) that makes a cube.
levels.b: Finds the area of each different face of a box.
levels.c: Adds up all the faces to find a box's total surface area.
levels.d: Finds the surface area of a pyramid from its flat pattern.

III.8.12.what: Finding volume, the space inside a 3D shape, for boxes and other prisms (shapes with the same cross-section all the way through).

levels.a: Counts the small cubes that fill a box.
levels.b: Multiplies the area of the base by the height.
levels.c: Finds the volume when edge lengths are fractions.
levels.d: Works backwards from the volume to find a missing length.
levels.e: Counts how many whole cubes really fit in a box, since leftover gaps can't hold one.
levels.f: Finds a box's volume from just the areas of its three different faces.

III.8.13.what: Finding the volume of a cylinder, like a can: the circle's area times the height.

levels.a: Multiplies a given base area by the height.
levels.b: Finds the circle's area first, then multiplies by the height.
levels.c: Starts from the width instead of the radius and gives an exact answer.
levels.d: Solves real problems, like how much a can holds.

III.8.14.what: Finding the volume of cones and spheres (balls), and how they compare with cylinders.

levels.a: Sees that three cones of water fill a cylinder of the same size.
levels.b: Finds a cone's volume as one third of the matching cylinder.
levels.c: Finds the volume of a sphere using its formula.
levels.d: Compares a cone, sphere, and cylinder of the same width and height.

III.8.15.what: The Pythagorean theorem: in a right triangle, the two short sides squared add up to the longest side squared.

levels.a: Names the hypotenuse, the longest side opposite the square corner.
levels.b: Finds the longest side from the two shorter ones.
levels.c: Finds a shorter side from the other two.
levels.d: Solves real problems, like how high a leaning ladder reaches.
levels.e: Finds the right triangles hidden inside a shape, like a diamond, to work out a side or an area.
levels.f: Works out how far the top of a ladder slides down when its foot slides out.

III.8.16.what: Using the Pythagorean rule in reverse to test whether a triangle has a square corner.

levels.a: Tests whether three side lengths make a right triangle.
levels.b: Recognizes Pythagorean triples, whole-number sets like 3, 4, 5 that make right triangles.
levels.c: Decides if a triangle's widest angle is smaller than, equal to, or larger than a square corner.
levels.d: Tests for a right angle when sides are decimals or the triangle is drawn on a grid.

III.8.17.what: Using the Pythagorean theorem to find the straight-line distance between two points on a grid.

levels.a: Counts squares to find the across and up legs of a right triangle.
levels.b: Works out those leg lengths from the points' coordinates.
levels.c: Finds the straight distance between two points.
levels.d: Finds the perimeter of a shape drawn on a grid.

III.8.18.what: Using the Pythagorean theorem to find slanted lengths in 3D shapes like boxes and cones.

levels.a: Finds the diagonal across one face of a box.
levels.b: Finds the diagonal from one corner of a box to the far opposite corner.
levels.c: Finds the slanted side length of a cone.
levels.d: Solves real problems, like the longest stick that fits in a box.

III.8.19.what: A translation slides a shape without turning or flipping it.

levels.a: Slides a shape on a grid and says where a corner lands.
levels.b: Uses a coordinate rule, like add 4 to each number, to slide a point.
levels.c: Knows a slide changes position only, not size, shape, or direction.
levels.d: Decides whether one shape is a slide of another.

III.8.20.what: A reflection flips a shape over a line, like a mirror image.

levels.a: Flips a shape over the horizontal axis.
levels.b: Flips a shape over the vertical axis.
levels.c: Flips a shape over the diagonal line where x and y are equal.
levels.d: Finds the mirror line between a shape and its reflection.

III.8.21.what: A rotation turns a shape around a fixed point, like the hands of a clock.

levels.a: Turns a shape a quarter turn about the center of the grid.
levels.b: Turns a shape a half turn.
levels.c: Turns a shape three quarters of a turn, paying attention to direction.
levels.d: Picks the coordinate rule that describes a turn.

III.8.22.what: A dilation enlarges or shrinks a shape by a scale factor, keeping its shape the same.

levels.a: Finds new lengths when a shape is enlarged.
levels.b: Finds new lengths when a shape is shrunk.
levels.c: Finds the scale factor from a point and its new position.
levels.d: Knows angles stay the same while area grows by the scale factor times itself.
levels.e: Works back from the change in area to the scale factor, remembering area grows by its square.
levels.f: Finds the fixed center point of a dilation from two points and where they end up.

III.8.23.what: Congruent shapes are exact copies; similar shapes are the same shape but possibly a different size.

levels.a: Knows slides, flips, and turns keep size the same, and only a dilation changes it.
levels.b: Decides whether two rectangles are similar by checking their proportions.
levels.c: Follows a sequence of moves to find where a point ends up.
levels.d: Decides whether two triangles are similar by checking two of their angles.
